Oficiali din domeniul informațiilor au declarat pentru FT că “mai este mult până se va putea face o atribuire concretă a amenințărilor”, dar unii membri ai comunității europene de informații cred că Rusia este cel mai probabil vinovat, invocând motivul, metoda, precedentul și primele indiciile criminalistice.

O componentă cheie a războiului hibrid al Rusiei este exploatarea vulnerabilităților civile într-un mod care poate fi negat, pentru perturbarea vieții de zi cu zi și pentru a încerca să arate cetățenilor europeni că guvernele lor nu ar fi incapabile să îi protejeze.

O ipoteză de lucru în rândul serviciilor de informații europene – care au discutat despre atacuri în ultimele zile – este că amenințările coordonate au fost produse de activiști pro-Kremlin sau de grupuri de hackeri. Dar, chiar și așa, tot nu este clar ce rol, dacă există vreunul, ar fi putut juca serviciile de informații rusești în direcționarea, încurajarea sau autorizarea unei astfel de activități.

Pack for tomorrow, not yesterday. A physicist says time travel to the past could be impossible.

A question many of us have posed in our minds is: where would you go if you had a time machine?

Would you crank the dial backwards like Marty McFly and risk sabotaging your own future? Before you start packing, a physicist has some news that may ruin a few Marvel movies: you may only be able to go one way, and it isn't backwards.

Hongsheng Zhang, a researcher at the University of Jinan in China, has shown that in a broad class of theoretical universes, travelling into your own past is impossible.

The whole argument rests on one fact. In relativity, the direction of light can never sit at right angles to an object’s direction through time.

Imagine spacetime sliced into layers that light itself can travel along. Anything moving slower or faster than light must cross these surfaces in the same direction, like climbing a staircase that never lets you step down.

If you can only ever go up, you can never arrive back on the step where you started.

The argument needs no exotic matter, no quantum effects and no assumptions about what fills the universe. "The whole content is bookkeeping about directions," Zhang told ScienceAlert.

The two loopholes

Physicists call journeys to the past "closed timelike curves": routes through spacetime that loop back to the very place and moment they began. Einstein's equations allow them in a handful of scenarios, such as near the core of a spinning black hole.

Crucially, Zhang's research - which is awaiting peer review - also reveals exactly how a time machine could achieve travelling back in time, and it claims there are only two ways.

The first is twist. Imagine light rays that, instead of travelling side by side, spiral around one another like the strands of a rope. When that happens, the neat surfaces of light can't form, so there is no one-dimensional staircase to keep you climbing.

This is what happens near the centre of a spinning black hole. Einstein’s theory says a spinning mass drags space and time around with it, an effect NASA’s Gravity Probe B satellite measured around Earth in 2011. Close to the black hole’s core the drag is so strong that moving “forward in time” is bent into a circle.

A traveller following that circle would see their clock ticking forward in time as normal, yet their journey would arrive back at the moment they set off. Physicist Brandon Carter showed in 1968 that such loops exist inside spinning black holes.

The second is the shape of the universe itself. The staircase might be perfectly built, but it could lead around the sides of a building, so the top step leads straight back to the bottom, like the impossible staircases in an Escher drawing. You would keep climbing and still end up where you began. Most of the time machines physicists have designed on paper, including those built from wormholes, rely on this trick.

The theorem has its limits, as Zhang acknowledges.

“What it does not do is tell us whether nature permits any of this. That remains open, and it is the question I would most like to see answered,” Zhang explained to ScienceAlert.

Destination: tomorrow

Trips to the future, by contrast, are already well established. Einstein showed that moving very fast, or sitting in strong gravity, slows your clock relative to everyone else's. Astronauts aboard the International Space Station return to Earth a few thousandths of a second younger than they would otherwise have been, according to the European Space Agency.

The work does not settle whether our own universe allows a journey to the past.

For now, though, anyone planning a trip may want to pack for tomorrow rather than yesterday... unless you have the Time Stone of course.

A prolonged period of cloudy and windless weather can throttle Europe's solar and wind generations, often causing the grid to rely on polluting back-up sources.

Europe risks entering its first ‘dunkelflaute’ of the year as cloudy weather dampens the continent’s solar boom and sends energy prices soaring.

Solar, which has been described as a “shining star” of the transition away from fossil fuels, is one of the quickest-to-install and cheapest forms of energy in the world. In the right conditions, it can cost as little as €0.024 to produce one unit of power via solar panels – far outperforming coal, gas and even wind.

It has already saved the EU €42.9 billion in avoided gas imports since the beginning of the war on Iran, which broke out on 28 February. It also helped stabilise the grid in the summer when back-to-back heatwaves triggered a spike in cooling-related electricity consumption.

But Europe’s prolonged period of cool, cloudy and windless weather pose a serious problem.

Can solar power perform in winter?

A dunkelflaute – German for ‘dark lull’ – is a term used to describe an extended period when wind and solar power generation are low or non-existent because there is not enough wind or sunlight.

It typically occurs from October through February in Northern Europe, exacerbated by short daylight hours, heavy cloud cover and fog. This coincides with increased energy consumption across the continent, due to chilly temperatures triggering demand for heating.

Multi-day dunkelflauten are rare, but such an occurrence pushes Europe’s energy grid to rely more heavily on expensive backup generation such as natural gas.

According to Bloomberg forecasts, German day-ahead power prices for Thursday 29 October were above €300 a megawatt-hour, about double the average in October, with hourly rates hitting above €500 for the evening peak.

‘It’s extremely disheartening’: Home solar output dips

On an individual scale, households with solar panels are also noticing a spike in their energy bills. One UK resident who has 12 solar panels installed on their roof with a combined capacity of 6.36 kW tells Euronews Earth that on Wednesday (4 November) the panels only produced 10.90 kWh of solar – leaving them to rely on the grid for an additional 27.40 kWh of energy required.

On Thursday (5 November), when their city was overcast for the entire day, the home generated just 2.40 kWh of solar, and imported 20.60 kWh.

This is despite having an 11.52 kWh home storage battery that is charged at night on an off-peak tariff to discharge in the day when electricity consumption increases.

Cloud is expected over the weekend and well into next week, meaning many Brits will be generating significantly less solar than they have during the summer.

“We’re hardly producing any power,” the resident, who wishes to remain anonymous, tells Euronews Earth.

“It’s extremely disheartening to see we’re importing so much energy when we have spent thousands on a solar system. However, we know that the panels will start to perform better when the clouds clear.”

Hydro steps in for solar’s dips

Of course, it is no surprise that solar produces most of its electricity in the summer months. In the EU, solar’s share of electricity generation hit 25.4 per cent in June – but in October this dropped to just 13.2 per cent.

Of course, solar relies on daylight opposed to heat - meaning homeowners with rooftop panels will still produce power even on cold days.

According to green energy supplier Good Energy, home solar systems in the UK can still generate around 25-35 per cent of their annual output in winter, which it says "provides a nice cushion for winter bills".

A dip in solar production also tends to coincide with increased generation of hydropower – which started to rise in the EU last year from October.

Solar is also able to help offset some of the electricity spikes caused by heatwaves, following a sudden need for space cooling, such as air conditioning and fans.

According to energy think tank Ember, during the late-June heatwave this summer, daily electricity demand rose by up to 28 per cent in Italy, 23 per cent in Hungary, 14 per cent in France and 13 per cent in Spain compared with pre-heatwave days.

It says that as heatwave-driven demand increased, solar was the only major power source to perform “better than usual”. Compared with other days in June and July, average daily solar generation during the heatwaves was 17 per cent higher in France and Hungary, five per cent higher in Spain and the same in Italy.

A typical UK home with rooftop solar generated enough electricity to power an A/C unit for five hours per day during the hot spell, a separate Ember analysis found.

At the same time, water-intensive forms of energy such as coal, hydropower and nuclear struggle during heatwaves – as scorching temperatures and lack of rainfall increase cause prolonged periods of drought.

In August, Poland was forced to reduce output on its coal-fired power plants, which require massive amounts of water for cooling, following critically low water levels in the Vistula River.

The move temporarily removed 1.3 GW from Poland’s power system, enough to power more than one million average households. This is around two per cent of the country’s current energy capacity.

From taking your shoes off indoors to being on time, a new survey reveals the social etiquette rules that travellers should know before heading to Europe.

A kiss on the cheek, turning up early or leaving food on your plate... little gestures can mean very different things across Europe.

Now, new research has revealed the etiquette rules travellers should know before heading to Europe, from greeting strangers to getting dinner right.

Preply, an online language learning and tutoring marketplace, looked at public data sources and surveyed 1,600 people living in 27 countries about European etiquette, and the results challenged some assumptions we’ve all probably been guilty of making.

While it might seem like etiquette isn’t a huge deal, it’s actually an important thing to consider when travelling to a country, where you’ll want to be kind, understanding and respectful of the people you meet.

It seems as though more people are understanding the necessity of the practice – and the proof is in the data.

As of September 2026, the #etiquette hashtag had reached some 4.4 billion views on TikTok, while searches for “how to have good etiquette” have risen by a staggering 373% in the past year alone.

When travelling in Europe, though, etiquette can change as quickly as the borders do, so it’s wise to be aware in order not to put a foot wrong. Here’s what the findings showed.

How to greet someone appropriately

You might associate Europeans with cheek kissing as a greeting, but it’s actually far less common than you might expect.

In 23 of 27 countries, the majority of people surveyed would actually wait for the other person to initiate two cheek kisses.

Across Europe, that figure is 85% and in Denmark, Estonia, Sweden, and Slovenia, respondents said they would reject the gesture outright.

Shoes on or off?

While not every country is as strict as Sweden – which saw 100% of respondents say it’s a must – taking off your shoes is common practice across the continent.

In 24 out of the 27 countries, most people said they would take their shoes off when visiting someone’s home.

Many countries in the north of Europe said indoor shoe removal was a must, and it was just Spain, Italy, and Portugal that disagreed, saying they preferred to keep their shoes on inside the home. That’s possibly down to warmer climates, which means houses have fewer carpets to protect.

Interestingly, there was an age divide, too.

Most respondents aged between 18 and 34 said they always took their shoes off, while those aged 35 to 54 preferred to wait until asked by the host.

To bring a gift or not to bring a gift?

Everyone likes to receive a gift from a visitor, but some like it more than others.

More than half of the survey respondents considered bringing a gift to be standard practice, while a third said they reserve gift-giving for special occasions.

Only Finland saw the majority say they’d never bring a host a gift.

The study found that respondents from 17 out of the 27 countries said they’d likely bring a bottle of wine or a bouquet of flowers when visiting a friend, although nine of that number – including Austria, the UK and Spain – said they’d reserve the gesture for a special occasion.

Make sure to finish your food

While opinions differ on most etiquette topics across Europe, finishing food was considered respectful across all 27 countries.

Seen as a universal marker of respect for the host’s effort, 82% of men said they always finished meals, compared to 75% of women.

Some female respondents said they were more likely to deliberately leave a little left, possibly out of a sense of politeness.

Punctuality is a divisive issue

Online searches for the term “is it better to be on time, early or late?” were, according to Preply, up 66% globally over the past year, and the data reveals a somewhat complicated answer.

In 23 out of 27 countries, respondents favoured arriving on time, with Greece particularly keen on punctuality, while 35% of men said they prefer to arrive early, a higher figure than female respondents who aim to arrive on time.

Respondents in Czechia, Germany, Poland, and France said they preferred to arrive early at a destination.

The survey found that single people were twice as likely to arrive late, and those with children found it particularly hard to keep to a rigid schedule.
